blocks.text: In a Dutch main clause the conjugated verb is always the second element. The first place can be the subject, but also a time word, a place or an object. If something else comes first, the subject moves to just after the verb. This is called inversion.

blocks.title: Not like English: no 'Tomorrow I go'
blocks.text: English says Tomorrow I go to London, with the subject before the verb. In Dutch that is wrong: the verb must be second, so the subject jumps behind it: Morgen ga ik naar Londen. Count the elements: Morgen (1), ga (2), ik (3).

blocks.title: Time before place
blocks.text: In the rest of the sentence, the usual order is time – manner – place: Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Utrecht. English often does the opposite: I'm going to Utrecht by train tomorrow.
A yes/no question starts with the verb: Ga je mee? A question with a question word starts with that word, followed directly by the verb: Waar woon je? Dutch never needs do.

head: Question
English
Answer
rows: What time does the film start?

blocks.text: Use geen instead of een, or before a noun without an article: Ik heb geen auto. Ik drink geen koffie. Use niet in all other cases. The place of niet depends on what it belongs to.

head: Rule
Example
English
rows: at the end, after the verb and the object
geen before a noun with een
The verb is always in second place.
After a question word: the verb.
Before a noun with een: geen.
niet after the verb and the time word.
